problem-type.h: WHAT KIND OF PROBLEM IS THIS?
problem-type.t: Each customer either **churns (1) or stays (0)**, so this is **binary classification**. That narrows the choice to classifiers, but there are still several ways to build one.

baseline.t: The first card is a **simple rule**: flag customers inactive for over 30 days. It reaches **0.81 accuracy but only 0.40 recall**, so it misses most churners. Any model has to beat this bar.

linear-model.t: The **logistic-style model** gives each feature a weight (blue pushes toward staying, red toward churn) and combines them. It is fast and **easy to explain**, which matters to retention staff.

tree-model.t: The **tree-style model** asks a chain of yes/no questions, such as idle days above 20, then tickets above 2. It can capture **combinations of signals**, but it is more flexible and harder to keep stable.

complexity.t: The bars rank the candidates by complexity: **1, 2, 3**. More flexible models can fit more patterns, including accidental ones, and they have **more to tune and more that can go wrong**.

interpretability.t: Retention staff need to understand **why** a customer is flagged. All three candidates can be explained when kept small, so interpretability does not rule any of them out.

constraints.t: The bar at the bottom lists the practical limits: staff must understand a flag, scoring runs **once a day** so speed is not critical, and we have only **700 training customers**.

candidate-set.t: The question marks show that we have **not chosen a winner**. Each card is a hypothesis to test, and a fancier model is not automatically a better one.

choose-to-test.t: All three go forward to be **trained and measured on the same validation set**. **Remember:** choose candidates by problem type, data size and constraints, then let the evidence decide.
